paragraphs.heading: A gas-filled float
paragraphs.text: A swim bladder is an organ inside bony fish that is filled with gas. Its job is to control how buoyant the fish is, so it can stay at the depth it wants without swimming to hold itself up, which would burn more energy. It is usually made of two gas-filled sacs in the dorsal part of the body, though a few primitive species have just one sac. Its walls are flexible, so they shrink or swell as the pressure of the surrounding water changes.

paragraphs.heading: Keeping the gas in
paragraphs.text: The bladder walls carry very few blood vessels and are lined with crystals of guanine, which stop gases from passing through. By changing the gas pressure inside, with the help of a gas gland or a structure called the oval window, the fish can reach neutral buoyancy. That lets it climb and sink across a wide range of depths. Because the bladder sits high in the body, it also steadies the fish from side to side.

paragraphs.heading: Gulpers and sealed bladders
paragraphs.text: In fish with a physostomous bladder, a tube called the pneumatic duct still joins the bladder to the gut. These fish fill the bladder by gulping air, and they can get rid of extra gas the same way. In more derived fish, the physoclisti, that link to the gut is lost. Young physoclists have to swim up to the surface to fill their bladders. Later the duct vanishes, and a gas gland must add gas, usually oxygen, to swell the bladder and lift the fish.

paragraphs.heading: How the gas gland works
paragraphs.text: The process starts when the gas gland gives off lactic acid and makes carbon dioxide, and the carbon dioxide turns the blood in a structure called the rete mirabile acidic. That acid makes the blood's hemoglobin let go of its oxygen, an effect named the Root effect, and some of the oxygen seeps into the bladder. On its way back, the blood passes through the rete mirabile again, and nearly all the spare carbon dioxide and oxygen cross over to the arteries feeding the gland. This countercurrent multiplication loop can build oxygen to a very high pressure, enough to explain gas in the bladders of deep-sea fish such as the eel, which needs hundreds of bars.

paragraphs.heading: Rising, sinking and bursting
paragraphs.text: At the oval window, the bladder touches the blood again, and oxygen can seep back out. Physoclist bladders have one serious drawback: the fish cannot rise quickly, or the bladder would burst. Fish with an open duct can burp gas out instead, but that makes it harder for them to dive again.

paragraphs.heading: Hearing and making sound
paragraphs.text: In some species, mostly freshwater fish such as carp and catfish, the bladder is linked to the inner ear. The link is a chain of four small bones called the Weberian ossicles, which pass vibrations on to the saccule and the lagena. In the red-bellied piranha, the bladder may act as a resonator.

paragraphs.heading: From lungs to bladders
paragraphs.text: Swim bladders and lungs share an evolutionary origin. The first lungs appeared in the common ancestor of ray-finned fish and lobe-finned fish, as pouches off the upper gut that let these animals gulp air when the water held little oxygen. In the Actinopteri, the ray-finned fish other than the bichirs, those lungs turned into the swim bladder. Unlike lungs, which grow out from the lower side of the gut, the bladder buds from the upper side of the front gut.

paragraphs.heading: Fish that do without
paragraphs.text: Sharks and rays have no swim bladder, because they belong to an entirely separate evolutionary branch. Most of them can only stay at a depth by swimming, which produces lift. Others store fats that are less dense than seawater, which leaves them close to neutral buoyancy, though they cannot easily adjust it as depth changes. In bony fish, the boundary between gas and tissue at the bladder reflects sound strongly, and sonar uses that echo to find fish.
